utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. We have been alerted that the Prosecution has a preliminary matter to raise. The Chamber itself has a preliminary matter which it wishes to address, but before that I take the appearance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. For the Office of the Prosecutor I'm Tom Hannis along with Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The matter which the Chamber wishes to raise is this, yesterday the -- we were apprised of the proposal of the Prosecution to place in evidence, presumably through the witness at present on the stand, this document which they only recently were able to tender -- to seek to tender in evidence, notwithstanding that they would have been aware of the possibility of this at an earlier stage, and as far as the Chamber is aware, neither the Chamber nor the other side was alerted to this. But be that as it may, there is a procedural difficulty in as much as the Prosecution having closed -- having completed its examination-in-chief of the present witness and documents not merely coming in by migration, as it were. The Chamber suggests that the procedural rules be tweaked, as it were, to invite or to allow the Prosecution to interpose at this stage the -- or interpose is the wrong word. To re-open its examination-in-chief interrupting the cross-examination of Mr. Zecevic which is in process to deal with that document, and then after which Mr. Zecevic, followed by Mr. -- would resume his cross-examination, followed by Mr. Pantelic. Before the Chamber formally so orders, do counsel on either side have a view as to that procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had been thinking about that and thought that I would probably have to seek leave to re-open if I wanted to show this document to Dr. Nielsen. I also thought about the possibility that perhaps later on the Prosecution would try to introduce this remaining document that we had to get provider permission to use, that we try to do it through a bar table motion or with a later witness. I can do it now as the Court suggests, that might be the most expedient. I'm happy to do that if that's agreeable with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was our understanding exactly that due to the fact that this document was provided under Rule 70 basis, that is why it came out so late in the proceedings, and it was our understanding that Mr. Hannis will not be using this document with this witness. However, if he intends to use this document with this witness, and direct him through this, then the only applicable solution, I think, would be what Your Honours have suggested, that he re-opens the case and then we continue the cross-examination. We wouldn't have a problem with that. Talking on behalf of Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know why I thought that he would not be using it in respect of this witness, but I may be mistaken. Perhaps he can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we made our original application to add, I think it was 17 documents to use with this witness. This document was on that list until we realised that it was a Rule 70 document that we hadn't yet received permission to use in this case. Then we filed an amended application removing that one and seeking leave to admit 16 other documents related to the issue of the Cutileiro plan and discussions and communications about that. So it was originally intended to be part of that whole package, but because we didn't receive it in time and didn't actually have permission until we completed direct exam of Dr. Nielsen, I didn't know what to do other than to seek permission to add it and then try and figure out the best time and way and possible witness to introduce it through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But bottom, you did intend to use it with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Originally, because it seemed to me a logical part of that whole --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: At this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Hannis. How much time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, five minutes, I would just ask Dr. Nielsen if he had seen this document and how did he see it as fitting in with the other documents in his view of whether or not the proposed separation and creation of a new Serb MUP was part of a Cutileiro plan or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, do you have a view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have objection to this way, to this proceedings. However, it's not being deal, I think Mr. Hannis will be mindful in terms of timing if he -- Prosecution will take these five or ten minutes, and we are still, I don't know, 15 minutes on, maybe, then tomorrow we could reserve -- we should do our best to finish today, but you know, every minute is counting. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So the Chamber rules that the Prosecution may be permitted to re-open its examination-in-chief in order to put this document to the witness who is at present on the stand. Could the usher escort Dr. Nielsen back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, during this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Written reasons for this ruling will follow in course. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry, in the meantime, Your Honour, with your permission, I would kindly request the Chamber to allow us the same position in approach with cross-examination like Stanisic Defence because we split certain topics, and Mr. Krgovic will take first part of cross-examination, then I will finish with the other line. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other matter that I wanted to raise, and it seems somewhat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I forgot -- when I asked for the witness to be returned, I forgot that you, yourself, had a matter. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I feel a bit ungracious raising it at this time, but it relates to the disclosure of documents to be used and cross-examined by the Zupljanin Defence. Last night at 6.20 I received an e-mail listing some 27 new documents that I had previously not been notified of. The original notification was received on December 14th when Mr. Nielsen started testifying, at that time there was a list of nine documents. On the 16th of December, three additional documents were notified. But now I have 27 new documents, and I just want to issue a complaint about this. You know, it's been a month since he was here, I don't understand why it had to wait until last night at 6.20 to be advised of these 27 new documents. And I note that two of them are listed as still awaiting translation. You will recall that witness Nielsen was delayed from testifying in September until December for the reason that there were hundreds of documents that the Defence said they needed to have translated before they could do his cross-examination. And frankly, I haven't seen that many translated documents used in the cross-examination so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these documents notified as going to be used for Mr. Nielsen are mainly notes from his report, and I may be using them during cross-examination because they concern certain answers provided by Mr. Nielsen to Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Cvijetic. All these documents that I will be using that are on that list are Prosecutor documents. Ninety-nine per cent of them have already been exhibited in this case. Nielsen in his report mentions them. So the Prosecution is not really taken by surprise nor are they really going to be prejudiced by my use of these documents. I indicated in my initial submission that I will be also using the Prosecution's documents for Mr. Nielsen. Most of my documents are in fact on the Prosecution list. The list of documents the Prosecutor indicated he would be using with Mr. Nielsen, and they are part of his package, so I don't think the Prosecution's objection is really well grounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: What about the -- you said 99 per cent, what about the maybe 1 per cent which Mr. Hannis says have not yet been translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, those are documents that were provided to the Prosecution back in December. All the documents I will be using have been translated. This is just part of the wider list and footnotes. I went through them and noted that some have not been translated, and those I will not be using. Because when my case manager was making up this list of documents, I did not know that some of these documents do not have translations, and those I will not be using in my cross-examination today. It's not my habit to use many documents in my examinations, especially not expert witnesses of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krgovic, would a fair summary of your response to the Prosecution be that Mr. Hannis' apprehensions have no real basis and we can proceed, there should be no difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] I just received information from my case manager that all the documents on my list are in fact documents referenced in the footnotes of Mr. Nielsen, even that one document which seemed to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's the case, Your Honour, I don't have any problem with that because I certainly need to be familiar with the documents that are in Mr. Nielsen's report. But when I receive a list first thing when I come in, in the morning, and it's not in numerical order, all I have is list of document ID numbers, I don't know what it is, that's and why I raised my complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could the usher escorted Dr. Nielsen to the stand, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Nielsen, I remind you that you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Zecevic resumes his cross-examination, the Chamber has ruled that the Prosecution be permitted to re-open its examination-in-chief in order to deal with certain documents which they have only recently come to be in a position to put to you. So I would now invite Mr. Hannis to deal with that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nielsen, there's just one document I want to ask you about. It's 65 ter number 3464. Your Honours, I'm advised by my case manager it's not in e-court yet, but we can use Sanction to bring it up on the screen for the witness. And this relates to the issue, Dr. Nielsen, that we talked about concerning the Defence position that the separation of the MUP and the creation of a separate Serbian MUP was, according to them, pursuant to an agreement or part of the Cutileiro plan or agreement. You recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this document is one letter that we had that was not available to us when you were doing your direct testimony back in December. Waiting to see if we can get it up through Sanction for you. Do you see that on your screen now? It's a document dated the 12th of June, 1992, from Mr. Cutileiro to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if you had a chance to see that document before you began your testimony?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that that is a document that I have seen before testifying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And based on the date of that document, 12 June 1992, and the content, can you tell us what your view is regarding this letter in connection with the claim that the separation and creation of separate Serbian MUP was being done pursuant to the so-called Cutileiro agreement or plan?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is one of the documents upon which I base my conclusion that it is erroneous to refer to a Cutileiro plan or agreement. As I stated repeatedly, I regard what Mr. Cutileiro was pursuing as a framework for further negotiations, and I think that Mr. Cutileiro's document or letter of the 12th of June, 1992, which we have in front of us here, confirms precisely that, in the sense that he is telling Mr. or Dr. Karadzic that the only way to bring peace to Bosnia and Herzegovina is through negotiation and that territorial claims which have been pursued by force are totally unacceptable. He also in the final paragraph alluding to Mr. Karadzic's letters, notes that, "... no promises have been made and that we reached an agreement on the 18th of March on a set of principles. The validity of that agreement, however," - he goes on it to say - "can only be upheld if borders and competences of the contingent units be defined by negotiated consensus and not by force ..." Again that, to me, indicates that what Mr. Cutileiro thought was in place was a framework for negotiations and not a final agreement to divide the country internally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nielsen. I have no further questions, Your Honour, I would tender document 3464 and close my direct examination for the second time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P507, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nielsen, since in view of this supplementary examination-in-chief, we have not learned anything new with respect to your views already expressed by you, I'm going to pick up where I left off yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please look at P160. Can the witness please be given the binders with documents. That's number 10 in your binder. Can we please have page 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have reviewed this document, sir. It is a summary of a meeting of senior officials held in Belgrade on the 11th of June, 1992, and you have made several references to this document in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 20 in B/C/S and 21 in the English, we have the conclusions adopted at this meeting of the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 20 in B/C/S and page 21 in English in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can see -- please, page 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I opened e-court yesterday, I noticed that it was page 20 in the Serbian version. I have just been told that it's actually 23. I apologise. The English page is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see conclusion number 1. And in this conclusion the second sentence begins by saying: "In doing so, complete constitutionality legality must be ensured, as well as independence without the influence of individual groups, [indiscernible], or parties." Can you see that portion of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that it is obvious that the Ministry of the Interior and the minister in particular had a problem with certain number of outside influences coming from individuals, groups factions in the territory, and that is why they have highlighted this as a problem?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was indeed one of the major topics of discussion at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 27. I suppose that's page 30 in B/C/S and 27 in English. I'm talking about item 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you yesterday about deportation, and it's been dealt with in the last paragraph. You can see that here as one of the problems that is being discussed at this meeting of the 11th of July is the resolution of the problem of residents of certain villages moving out who are not within the jurisdiction of the MUP, but there is a desire to attribute this to the MUP. You would agree with me that that was also one of the problems that was very seriously discussed at this 11th of July meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly agree that that was a major topic of discussion. I would agree that not only in this document, but also in numerous other documents that I quote in my report, the MUP complains - and this goes back to Judge Harhoff's question of yesterday - the MUP complains that the army is without any selection criteria rounding up large numbers of especially Bosnian Muslims and that MUP uses the term "dumping" them in facilities which the MUP is then forced to guard or take care of, and indeed Mr. Zupljanin mentions this at this meeting. It's also reflected a week later in the instructions that are issued by the minister pursuant to this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will certainly agree with me, but thank you for this exhaustive answer, you will agree with me that it is obvious that these two facts that we have just discussed, that is the influence from certain individuals and the situation on the ground which involved the bringing in of a large number of Muslims and exerting pressure on the MUP to provide securities for such collection centres, and the moving out of people were problems, and that the MUP had a kind of negative attitude towards this, actually, they were criticizing this kind of conduct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, again, agree with you that this is one of the major problems that is faced by the Ministry of Internal Affairs in the summer of 1992. It is a problem that is frequently discussed. It is one of the reasons why already in July 1992 the RS Ministry of Internal Affairs is trying to transfer responsibility of detention facilities such as Omarska to the army. As I said, to get out of the business of running or being responsible for detention facilities. I would also note that it is of course the case that there are detention facilities established in the RS at this point which were established originally as police facilities and not by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you discussed this with my friend and you confirmed that Omarska, Keraterm, and the like had been set up pursuant to a decision issued by the Crisis Staff; is that right? You said that the fact was that a member of the police, Mr. Simo Drljaca, was a member of the Crisis Staff. Do you remember that response of yours?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simo Drljaca as a chief of the public security station of Prijedor municipality was a member of the Prijedor Crisis Staff, and he implemented not only that decision of the Crisis Staff but regularly implemented decisions of the Prijedor Crisis Staff, just as did his police colleagues at other Crisis Staffs in the country or in -- excuse me, in Republika Srpska in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that happened because that was done by the Crisis Staffs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand your question. Are you saying that people such as Mr. Drljaca made those decisions or implemented those decisions because they were themselves appointed by the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Simo Drljaca was appointed by the Crisis Staff and so was Mr. Vrucinic as well as a large number of individuals who were chiefs of public security stations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it is the case that a large number of police officials at the municipal level were appointed by the Crisis Staffs. However, the Crisis Staffs also in many cases confirmed the existing SRBiH MUP appointments of police officials, and most of the police officials who were appointed by the Crisis Staffs were later confirmed by RS MUP as employees of that ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 1993 and 1994 and onwards. Sir, isn't it true that in the instruction on the work of Crisis Staffs issued by the government of Republika Srpska - that's Exhibit P70, we don't need it on our screens - it is explicitly stated, and you have quoted this in paragraph 205 of your report, that "the command of the army and the police will remain in the hands of professional organs rather than the Crisis Staffs." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the case, and it is also the case that the role of Crisis Staffs is one of the most frequently discussed topics at meetings of the RS MUP in the course of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You certainly know that on the 23rd of May, that P270 requested for the Crisis Staffs to be disbanded and abolished, are you aware of that? I apologise for the transcript, it's P217. That's minutes of the meeting of the government session.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not personally aware of that. I would defer to my colleague's report on the Crisis Staffs on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this document, it's number 17 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit P217.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Item 4 reads, the minutes of the meetings of the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, item 4: "It has been concluded to undertake measures to abolish Crisis Staffs." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, that is what the document says. We both know that the Crisis Staffs, nevertheless, continued to exist for quite some time after that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. However, already on the 24th of May, there was an attempt to set up War Presidency and then on the 31st of May, Karadzic again ordered War Presidency to be set up, and then the Serbian Democratic Party on the 31st of May insisted on the Crisis Staffs to be abolished, and then on the 10th of June Karadzic came up with a new proposal or, rather, an order to establish war commissioner offices. Is this how this process concerning Crisis Staff developed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that what you just summarised is reflected in the report of my colleague, Ms. Hanson, and also the report of Patrick Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact is also that in the September amendments to the constitution, abolished the Crisis Staffs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't doubt that. That would be accurately reflecting the trend in the summer of 1992, which is to centralise power and to abolish decision-making, or restrict decision-making, rather, at the municipal and regional levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for reference, that the amendment to the constitutions are Exhibit 1794 according to 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, a slight digression, in paragraph 212 and your footnote 255, we discussed yesterday the statements made by politicians and what kind of influence it had and what kind of weight they carry with regard to other documents. In paragraph 212 and the footnote 255, you quote a letter sent to the media written by Mr. Mico Stanisic in April 1992. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this letter, he speaks about -- and this is what you cite in your report, about over 4.000 active-duty policemen and several tens of thousands of reserve police officers who were keeping under control about 70 per cent of the territory. This is what the letter states; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the letter in front of me, but, yes, that's how I've quoted it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you have quoted this letter of his; however, at the same time several times in your report you cited 279 65 ter document. It's 28 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have it in e-court. 275 [as interpreted] according to 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the interpreter is asking if you could repeat the page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was away from the microphone. It's page 6 in B/C/S and page 8 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, number 28 in your binder is not 275 of the 65 ter list but is 279 of the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said 279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. In the record it's -- in the transcript it's 275.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you remember quoting this document several times in your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I have an entire section of the report about that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously in the Serbian version for some reason I have the wrong page. But since I don't have much time, the English pages -- good, now I'm been told that this is page number 10 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, in the original document it's page 6, the last paragraph, and in e-court it's the second paragraph from the top which says: "By the beginning of April, 12.000" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the English page was good, please, we had problem with the page in B/C/S. Can we please have page 8 in English, second paragraph from the top. We don't need anything else. Leave it as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It reads here that, in the final annual report of the MUP, that: "By the beginning of April, there were under 10.000 reserve police officers and almost 3.000 active duty policemen which makes a total of 12.600." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is apparently in contradiction with what Mr. Stanisic mentioned in his letter to the media, which he wrote as a politician. There's a huge difference. He mentions several tens of thousands, whereas in this official document, we have the figure which is below 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object. That's misleading. The statement by Mr. Stanisic was on the 18th of April. The report is referring to the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Hannis, even if we are talking about early April or the first half of April, if you think that in three days alone you can recruit many tens of thousands, then obviously we have a problem. Can the witness answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it to admit that I'm a bit surprised that you are characterising Mr. Stanisic as a politician, when I understand that you are in fact trying to portray him as a professional police officer. The fact of the matter is that he said what he said on the 18th of April, 1992. If it is the case that he is exaggerating compared to what is in the RS MUP 1992 annual report, then I certainly accept that point. I would point out that in paragraph 212, I do not comment at all on Mr. Stanisic's statement. I just say that that is what he stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm extremely grateful to you. All I'm asking is why in your paragraph 212 you did not provide any comment on these facts that I have just put to you, unlike what Mr. Stanisic quoted in his letter to the media, in this annual report we have completely different data. That was my question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary, it is I who am extremely grateful to you. I look forward to incorporating that more subtle point in the next version of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Nielsen, when you speak about Special Police units, primarily the Special Police brigade, isn't it true that this kind of formation as an anti-terrorist unit existed in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I state so in my report. There was one unit that existed in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this Special Police brigade commanded by Mr. Karisik was referenced by you in a document which is 1861, 65 ter, and that's number 30 in your binder. That is, in fact, a list relating to this unit from May 1992, and it is stated that it numbers 170 men.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. For purposes of clarity, we should just be very precise and note that Mr. Karisik was the commander of the RS MUP Special Police brigade and not the SRBiH MUP unit to which we previously referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In item 220 of your report, you say that this Special Police brigade of the RS MUP established its detachments in the territory attached to CSBs in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wrote is that in the course of the late summer of 1992, in the autumn of 1992, certain "Special Police units" that were swarming all over the RS, also at the CSB level, were largely disbanded with the intent to centralise Internal Affairs and consolidate control of the remaining special units under the charge of Mr. Karisik and the Special Brigade of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you will agree with me that at the time, i.e., from April until the end of summer 1992, it was fashionable, as it were, for everyone in every municipality to set up special detachment, intervention detachments and things like that, and this was mainly done by the Crisis Staffs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that it was the case. As I've stated previously, that virtually any person with a bit of weaponry, a few buddies, and surplus of testosterone was forming special units during the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are aware that, for example, in Trebinje there was a Special Police unit formed back in October 1991 when neither the MUP of Republika Srpska or nor Republika Srpska itself existed. This unit was headed by Alija Delimustafic. This unit actually didn't have a proper structure. They just gathered together, as you've just described, those were armed individuals, they proclaimed themselves to be Special Police units, and then they would go on to carry out looting and plunder.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly aware of the existence of Special Police units formed in the autumn of 1991 in the Trebinje east Herzegovina area. However, I'm not aware that any such unit was headed by Alija Delimustafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I said that it was created that at the time when the MUP minister of the SR B&H was Alija Delimustafic, and that is when neither the MUP nor Republika Srpska itself existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I believe that unit to which you are referring is in fact dealt with in the RS MUP draft annual report where it is noted that that unit was formed without the awareness of the officials in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, please wait for the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... 27th July, 1992, and that's 65 ter 307 in your binder 37. An order from Mr. Mico Stanisic dated 27 July. It's your number 37. Paras 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He orders that all special units established during the war in CSB areas be disbanded immediately and placed under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska along with all their members, and he says as the process of replenishing police units was under way, that's the Karisik brigade, all individuals who meet certain criteria may apply to be admitted into the platoons of this Special Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and I cite that document in the report for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to a new subject. The question of reporting, you deal with it in paragraph 236 and onwards. I must tell you that I found ten documents, orders and intercessions by the Ministry of the Interior beginning with 18 April, all the way up to October 1992, expressing frustration over the problem of deficits in reporting. Do you agree, having seen all this documentation, that there was a huge problem with reporting within the MUP, lack of reports by Security Services Centre and police stations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that communication was one of the major structural hurdles that RS MUP faced particularly in the summer of 1992. That is reflected not only in the draft annual report, it is reflected amply in the minister's comments in the 11 July 1992 meeting, and in fact, in the very fact that they were meeting in Belgrade because it was the only place they claimed that they could in fact meet at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I'd like you to go back to 65 ter 279, the one we just mentioned some time ago, the annual progress report. English page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm told by my colleagues that the answer of Mr. Nielsen is written into my previous question. I suppose his answer begins with the word "I agree" at 21, 18. Will this be enough to correct the transcript or shall I ask the witness to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you to go back to document 65 ter 279, and that's your -- it's in your binder. It's page 28, and in English it's page 23. It says there that on the average in all lines of work in the seat of the MUP, 15 dispatches were sent and 16 were received. That's the third paragraph on that page. In English it's the second paragraph from the top. "On average, 15 dispatches a day were sent..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that bearing in mind that there were five Security Services Centres, CSBs, and by the nature of things each CSB delivered its daily report at least once a day, and the CSBs also provided a daily report along the national security line, each CSB on average sent three dispatches or telegrams a day to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am quite sure that your arithmetic skills are better than mine. I would just note that helpfully the colleagues in RS MUP did the computations for us, and that still adds up to over 4.000 dispatches going in each direction over a nine-month period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, but that's precisely why I am presenting this to you. Two out of three every day are daily reports, so on all other issues only one report a day was sent by a CSB to the MUP to deal with all the other matters, all the other lines of work. I'm talking about average values, of course.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly understand your point. I would just note that the daily reports which you seem to be marginalising in your comments often contained, and indeed were supposed to on the minister's instructions, contain all of the critical information that the ministry needed to do its work on a daily basis. So I would not minimise the significance that they were receiving such reports. I would also note as an analyst that when we say one dispatch, that could be one sentence, it could also be a much larger dispatch. So it's very difficult to generalise here. My impression, certainly as an analyst given the mountains of documentation I had to hike through, is that there was a quite substantial amount of information exchange and communication going on during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were talking about these daily reports, have you ever compared the contents of these daily reports that arrived from the ground covering events and developments that were ongoing or had just happened on that territory, have you ever made that comparison?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have in some cases, for the sake of my own curiosity, made such a comparison. And I'm sure, like the minister, and as is reflected in the minister's admonishments to his subordinates, one can often be dismayed by the sparseness of the information provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding discipline, Mr. Nielsen, you discuss it in paragraph 227 of your report. Yesterday, my colleague mentioned 1D54, the rules on disciplinary responsibility adopted by Minister Stanisic. And you said, if I remember correctly, you had not reviewed these rules?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I said that I was familiar with the document, but that I had not reviewed the rules in detail in comparison to the earlier SRBiH rules on disciplinary responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So we cannot really discuss it, but if I tell you that this document, the rules adopted in the summer of 1992 on disciplinary responsibility shortened the dead-line for starting disciplinary proceedings and doubled the statute of limitations and simplified the procedure for establishing disciplinary responsibility making it speedier and more efficient, would you, from your expert point of view, consider that an adequate step by the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that I would like to comment on what I would consider adequate or inadequate. I would certainly agree provisionally, as I did already yesterday in answer to your colleague's question, that it does seem that they are streamlining the rules on disciplinary procedures, statutes of limitations and such. From my point of view, the major innovation or the most interesting innovation seems to be point number 1 in the 23rd July confidential order which I cite in paragraph 227 of my report, and that is, the move to transfer those employees of MUP who have committed criminal acts, except political and verbal misdemeanours, and to put them at the disposal of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, sir, you are certainly aware since you quote from these documents, that the document does not say that they are amnestied from their criminal or disciplinary responsibility?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the document in question does not offer an amnesty from criminal or disciplinary responsibility. And I know that this issue has been discussed previously in this trial. I would just note, and I give one very specific case, that of the deaths at Koricanska Stijena in August 1992 where the RS MUP's own investigation is effectively terminated merely because the officers suspected in participating in the killings at Koricanska Stijena are currently subordinated to the VRS and are involved in combat activities. That is the response that is given back up to the minister of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sure that the Zupljanin Defence will discuss the matter of Koricanska Stijena with you. However, the fact is that the criminal report about that event was filed to the competent prosecutor's Office and competent court. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall from other cases at this court that that is the case, and that those police officers who were already in August and September 1992 suspected in participating in those activities were not in fact prosecuted until much, much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the gist is this: The competent authorities did everything that they were duty-bound by the law to do at the time, and they filed a criminal report against an unidentified perpetrator long before they realised that there was police involvement in the event. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am, again, aware that a criminal report was filed. My account based on the available RS MUP documentation is to be found in paragraphs 327 and 328, but, yes, I am aware that such a report was filed. I note that on 14th September, 1992, Simo Drljaca, and I'm quoting here from page 327 of my report "... responded that an investigation could not be carried out because the officers who had participated in the convoy on 21 August were currently deployed on the battle-field." So that is what I meant by my earlier statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, you will probably discuss that with the Zupljanin Defence. The fact is that before the document you quote from, a criminal report had already been filed to the prosecutor and the court, whereas the police continued with their investigation trying to identify the people involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, the time that the Defence team of Mr. Zupljanin generously granted me has expired. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before you begin your cross-examination, there is a question which the Chamber in the person of Judge Harhoff has of Dr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And the reason I put this question to Mr. Nielsen at this point is to allow you, Mr. Zecevic, before we go on for the break, to use the answers that Mr. Nielsen is going to provide to my questions if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the question that I have for you, Mr. Nielsen, are two. Namely, first, there seem to be a duplicity in the answers that you gave to Mr. Zecevic regarding the information that was provided to the ministry from the institutions below. Namely, in your first answer in which you said that the flow of communication was poor, it was a big problem, it was discussed at every meeting throughout the summer and the early fall of 1992. And you ended up by saying that, well, maybe it was poor, the information, but certainly a substantial flow of information was in fact provided to the ministry from the institutions below it. First of all, of course, the CSBs. My second question is put to you as an expert on the MUP, namely, what was the system of digesting information in the MUP at the time? My question is really, the daily bulletins that came from various bodies in the field, so to say, and sent to the MUP, how were they treated and how were they synchronised and synthesized up through the ministry levels to the minister's desk? Do you know how this worked, and can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for your questions, Your Honour. The duplicity that you observe in the answers, as you put it, is in fact a duplicity that I'm reflecting as an analyst because it's present in the MUP's own documentation. It is not the -- the problems concerning information are not unique in this respect. There are a number of other problems that they discuss again and again and again, and clearly consider to be among the most substantial obstacles that they face. But where you see that on a day-to-day basis, they manage to get by, they manage to get the information that they need, they manage to get the job done, as it were, I would note that the daily bulletins that came from these various subordinate bodies in the field are only, as we discussed earlier, one type of information that is sent to the RS MUP. There is a very, very substantial amount of documentation. If you look at the collections that the Office of the Prosecutor for Prijedor, for Banja Luka, you can see on a daily basis things that start at the village level in the Prijedor area being reported up to the municipality, the SJB public security station level. Being reported on to the regional level in Banja Luka, and then being reported up to the ministry in Pale or Bijeljina as was the case, and the other way around. And of course, we see that things are being delivered by courier. We see that innovations are being made, such as at one point the need to bounce radio signals from eastern Herzegovina first through Montenegro and then back into Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to be able to communicate. But through various ingenious and creative methods such as these and the sheer weight and amount of documentation that we have been able to find for the period from April 1992 until the end of 1992, I, as an analyst, am left with the impression of a ministry in which communication was at times extremely difficult, but there was regularly ongoing communication because quick fixes and work-arounds were found to remedy a difficult situation on the ground. In response to your second question, without going into too much detail with specific respect to the daily bulletins, a lot of it was, as one can see, cut-and-paste work, so the -- once the reports start coming in the second half of April 1992, you can see a report that is being sent from Prijedor to Banja Luka, reporting on some incident or something that's relevant for the security in that operational area. The exact same sentence, literally verbatim, is cut and pasted into the report that the CSB in Banja Luka or Sarajevo or Trebinje sends up to the ministry, and that again, that exact same sentence, is then cut and pasted into the daily bulletin of the ministry itself, which the ministry was providing and had been asked to provide to the Presidency of the republic and to the government, and in some case, as I note in my report, this would also be sent to Belgrade so that authorities in Belgrade would be aware of what was ongoing. These reports, these daily bulletins as well as other information, was then collated, there was a specific analytical department within the MUP that was responsible and that exists to this day in the RS MUP, an analytical department which was responsible for collating, storing, and preserving these reports and producing the types of quarterly, semi-annual, and annual report that I also cite in my report. That kind of analytical informational department is present in the ministry itself. It's also present at the municipal and the regional level, and that's reflected in the rule book on internal organisation. So this is why we also at the municipal and regional level are getting quarterly and annual or, rather, in 1992 nine-month reports. So there is an ongoing collation of information, and there are responsible officials in the ministry whose job it is to make sure that long-term trends in, for example, crime are spotted and are directed to the attention of the appropriate officials in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just two questions, Your Honour. If I may ask my two questions and then take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Zecevic:

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you were looking at these daily reports submitted by the MUP to the Presidency and on, didn't you notice that in a great number of them there is a note, no reports available from two CSBs each day?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost certainly there are periods of two, even five days where, for example, Doboj would not be able to put a report through.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that there had been cases when some CSBs were not in contact with the ministry for two or three weeks on end?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there are periods in which some CSBs were, for example, without electricity. And that is the cases in which, as I know, previous witnesses have said who worked in the ministry work-arounds were found through couriers, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, but some areas were not accessible, even to couriers, and if anything is sent by courier, it can arrive ten days later. Just one more thing, since war is raging throughout the territory, the ministry from a territory of one CSB covering ten police stations receives one report per day. In your view does that really reflect the level of information available to the ministry in terms of its inadequacy?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not certain if -- which -- indeed if you are referring to a specific CSB in your question. But I think the most appropriate measuring stick is really if one goes through the analytical work of assembling in a database, as I have done all the dispatches going one way and going the other way, you see very considerable and regular traffic, and the bottom line is that if we take as the measuring stick this important 11 July 1992 meeting of all the leading officials of the ministry in which they are discussing all the most pertinent problems, we certainly see that in the middle of a raging war, as you put it, they are aware of all the most considerable problems confronting the ministry without the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One last question. That meeting of the collegium on the 11th July is the first meeting of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct because Mr. Zupljanin refers accurately, It's been a long time since we've seen each other in Sarajevo, he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I suppose he is referring to the time before the war, and that's why he says it's been a long time. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not precisely, because there was, in fact, and it's cited in my report, a collegium that did meet in, on, I believe, the 14th of April, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the collegium meeting in Drace when none of the representatives of other CSBs were present. I'm asking you about meetings of all CSB representatives together with the minister, that happened for the first time on 11th July?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with that consideration, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. We take the break now and resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm sorry, due to the haste I was cross-examining, I failed to -- I omitted to offer a certain document for admission. It's 65 ter 307, and I was commenting it with the witness and then I moved on. I would ask the Trial Chamber to admit this document as an MFI document, and I discussed that with my learned friend Mr. Tom Hannis from the Prosecution, due to the fact that there is a certain problem with the English translation of the original document. Therefore I would move the Trial Chamber to admit the document as an MFI pending additional reconsideration by the CLSS on the translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic. Which document is this, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 307. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit 1D176, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours, I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Would the usher kindly escort the witness back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. I'm on the Stojan Zupljanin Defence team, and I'm going to ask you a number of questions relating either to your report or to your evidence given so far in this case. In order to assist the Chamber since you understand our language, I would kindly ask you for us to pause between questions and answers to avoid overlapping, despite all the warnings coming from the Trial Chamber, I'm not very disciplined in that area, but let us try and make life easier for everyone. Mr. Nielsen, as far as I could discern from your CV and from your testimony so far, you have no formal education in the area of police matters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. My training is as a historian, not as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you didn't finish a police academy or any other similar course that deals with police matters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I've not taken any professional police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you have never worked in the police; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I have had the pleasure of working with the police, but not in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you have never been brought in by the police and you didn't have an opportunity to experience how the police operate, probably people who have frequent contact with the police have more familiarity with their work than ordinary citizens, wouldn't you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I certainly don't have a criminal record, but I do have some experience in how the police operates because I have on a number of occasions executed search warrants together with police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What I would like to establish before I ask you a question is the following: You also are neither a legal nor a military expert; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is crucial because sometimes you use some police terms and some military terms, and when you do so, how shall I put it, you construe them and understand them as an educated person or a person who is well educated. But when you do so, you provide your interpretation of these terms from your own angle; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do primarily look at these terms from the angle of a historian who, as I've noted previously, has extensively worked on police in the Yugoslavia -- former Yugoslavia. Where I'm in doubt in terms of military or police terms, I look particularly at the way the RS MUP, for example, itself uses those terms, and as you will see in my footnotes, on a number of occasions, I make reference to a Serbian dictionary of police terms. I should note as well, I think this is the appropriate time, that I was on one occasion in 2008 retained by the organisation for security and co-operation in Europe as an advisor to the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your report I have noticed in places that you are using the term a "war crime." Would you agree with me on that? Shall I give you a reference, a particular reference?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think a particular reference is necessary. I quite certainly recall that I did use that term, and my use of that term, as far as I recall, is analogous to my use of the term legal or illegal, that is to say, I'm not myself pretending or purporting to make any legal findings, rather I'm noting that that is the word used in the documents concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, as I understand your understanding of war crime, this is a crime committed during a state of war or during war; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I have certainly an understanding of what the legal definition of a war crime is. Stealing a bicycle in war time is, for example, as you well know, not a war crime, even though it takes place during a state of war or during a war. When I use -- again, when I use the term war crime, I do so, for example, in the context of when Minister Stanisic orders an investigation of what he calls war crimes or crimes against humanity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when a bicycle is stolen during a war by a Muslim or a Croat, would that constitute a war crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One of the indictments issued here is that aiding and abetting the destruction of Muslim houses was qualified as a war crime on the bases that nothing was done to prevent it.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am aware of the fact that plunder and looting, for example, is a war crime, and I suppose that the theft of a simple bicycle could be lumped into that category, given a very specific context. But I'm referring to the mere stealing of a bicycle on itself, even though it's war time, does not constitute a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We will go back to this issue. My learned friend Zecevic asked you yesterday about a portion of your report, that's your executive summary, paragraph 11 in B/C/S. I'm particularly interested in one sentence from that portion where you say that the RS MUP was the only armed force that was exclusively under the control of the authorities of Republika Srpska. Have you read this part of this findings of yours? My colleague Zecevic showed you yesterday and definitely in the course of your research you could see that in addition to the RS MUP pertaining to the period up to 12th of May 1992, there also existed the Serbian Territorial Defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of the existence of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it was also exclusively under the control of the authorities of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a very good question, and the reason, again, that I'm using the term solely under the control of the RS authorities for the RS MUP is precisely because it is my understanding based on the findings of my colleague who is a military expert, that the control of the TOs was very much a disputed topic during this period until the formation of the VRS and that there was an ongoing struggle between certain officials in the JNA and certain officials in the TO and the civilian authorities about who exactly was in control of these. I know that your colleague yesterday referred to the relevant military legislation which shows that the TO was under control of the JNA, and the JNA was certainly not solely under the control of the civilian authorities of the RS at this point. But again on this point, I would most certainly defer ultimately to a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the period up to the 12th of May when Republika Srpska was established. You are talking about control over the TO, and Colonel Basara testified about this issue as well, you probably had an opportunity to see his interview. Later a decision was made to resubordinate it to Army of Republika Srpska. However, in this document, the Territorial Defence, the Serbian Territorial Defence was a significant factor and was to a great extent under the control of the Serbian authorities. When I say the Serbian authorities, I'm referring to Mr. Subotic and the Ministry of Defence and the Presidency of Republika Srpska. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your statement that the Serbian Territorial Defence was a significant factor and was to a great extent under the control of the Serbian authorities. My only disagreement with you is whether they were under the sole control of the Serbian authorities, that is the RS authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in that respect would you like to amend your report by adding the Serbian TO which to a great extent was also under the control of the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, his report says that the RS MUP was the only one that was under the exclusive control of Serb authorities. He has just given his answer that the TO was not under the exclusive control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the documents shown to you by Mr. Zecevic and the ones that you have reviewed, did you find a single document, and I'm speaking about the period from April, and that is the 16th of April when the TO was formed, until the 12th May, 1992, have you found a single document testifying to the contrary that the TO was not under the control of the authorities of Republika Srpska? Actually, I put it to you that you didn't find any such document because you haven't -- otherwise you would have included it in your report.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, there are such indications in the intercepts that I've quoted in which you can see that the RS's civilian leadership, for example, is complaining about the fact that not all of the TO is doing precisely what the RS leadership might wish it to be doing, but ultimately, again, and I think this is the main point, I would certainly defer to the military expert on this issue. It is my understanding, and part of my conclusion in paragraph E11 is based on that, from his own report that there were disputes regarding the control of the TO during this period. I'm not disputing at all, I reiterate, I do not dispute that the Serbian civilian authorities had very extensive control of the TO during this period. I am disputing only and only disagreeing with you whether they had sole control of the TO during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you speak about these disputes, that was, in fact, a conflict to the effect that the Serbian TO was not obeying Subotic but rather the local officials and Crisis Staffs, and that they were acting in accordance with their instructions and orders?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly one form of concern. There's also concern expressed frequently by the RS leadership during this period that the TO is, to some extent, under the control of what they called "komunjara," old school communist cadres in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are certainly aware, I'm talking about the Banja Luka Krajina and all the other municipalities mentioned in the indictment and referred to my client, such as Sanski Most, Banja Luka, Donji Vakuf, Teslic, Kljuc, Prijedor, that the Serbian TO did exist?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm aware that a TO existed in all of those municipalities and that in many cases it adopted the monicker Serbian TO during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that in all of these municipalities, and let me remind you of the testimony given by the police station commander in Sanski Most, and the documents from the Sanski Most Crisis Staff which show that the control over the Serbian TO goes along the line Crisis Staff, the Serbian TO, and then upwards towards the level of the republic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we are going to have a reference to the testimony of a witness, can we have a page reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was speaking in general terms because it was mentioned at least 50 times and many documents were shown to that effect. I'm just asking the witness whether he is generally aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was my general question because I understood that you read certain witness statements and other documents, therefore, I concluded that you are aware of that without going into any specifics. I just wanted to ask you whether you agree with me or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we clarify the question. It means is the witness generally aware of the specific situation in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about these specific municipalities in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the question was referring specifically to the Sanski Most witness and Sanski Most. Now if he is expanding it to Donji Vakuf, Teslic, Kljuc, Prijedor, and Banja Luka, I think he needs to lay some more foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only asking the witness whether he was aware of that, he agreed with me that the situation was as described, and just as a reminder, I mentioned Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am aware that testimony on that point has been heard before this Chamber. I don't want to comment on the testimony of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But in the course of your research, you would agree with me that TO existed in all those municipalities and that it was under the control of the local Crisis Staff, or rather, subject to co-ordination?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware from the expert report of my colleague on Crisis Staffs that the Crisis Staffs were quite involved in the work of the TOs during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, before we move on to something else -- and I don't know if you are indeed moving on to something else, but that's the way it looked to me. But before we do so, I would like to solicit from the witness some indication of how did this work out in practice. You say that the TOs were partly, and perhaps even mostly, under the control of the Crisis Staffs and the local political authorities, and yet they were also to some extent under the control of the JNA. How did -- what was the practical way in which this could function? I mean, it sounds very complicated to have two such different organs both being in control of the same body. So how, what sort of co-ordination was in place in order to secure reasonable control over the TOs? Can you clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- with respect I'm not certain that I'm very well placed to answer your question. I base my knowledge of that subject on my reading of the expert reports of my colleagues Ewan Brown and Dorothea Hanson who have written respectively on the TOs and the Crisis Staffs, and as well on the MUP documents where I see a veritable tug of war going on during this period. I note that on direct examination we even saw one example of Mr. Stanisic issuing an order to the TO. So this is a period, up until the formation of the VRS, is a period in which everyone, Crisis Staffs, civilian leadership, police, military, are sticking their fingers, as it were, into the work of the TO. And it's only clarified, as counsel has noted, with later decisions and legislation passed by the RS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude, Mr. Nielsen, when you spoke about the Serbian MUP as the only force that was under control, since you are not a military expert, you didn't deal very much with the Serbian TO, the control of it, and its functioning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's why my report only on a few occasions alludes to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from that I deduce that your report in this part where you say that the Serbian MUP was the only organisation under the control of the RS should be taken with a certain reservation, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. He needs to include the term "exclusive" or "sole" control of the RS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I did. It's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you heard this, when you were writing your report you didn't take into consideration the position of the TO, and its place within this hierarchy, you didn't analyse the Serbian TO in that respect?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that this is a conclusion that I base on my reading of police and civilian documentation, particularly the discussions in the RS Assembly at the time. And to the extent that this -- that you disagree with my conclusion, I think it's most appropriate to put that question to the military expert to whom I would at any point defer. Again, I'm not disagreeing at all that there was extensive civilian control of the Serbian TO at this point. I am making a very narrow point here, which is just that, as far as I can see, the RS MUP -- and based on the apparently controversial statements of Mrs. Plavsic and other politicians, they treat the RS MUP as the only organisation under their exclusive control during this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further in the next paragraph, 13, there is another conclusion, the last sentence: "Towards the end of June 1992 in the MUP of Republika Srpska there were only six non-Serbs working." That's your conclusion, and you refer to paragraphs from 192 to 207. In these paragraphs you referred to a few documents on the basis of which you made this conclusion. Have you had the opportunity to look also at other documents mentioning different numbers as to the non-Serb employees in MUP? Without, however, including them into your report, without mentioning them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for that question. The specific number of six non-Serbs is taken from a specific RS MUP document which I cite in that passage in which I believe five of the six were actually working in Kalinovik of all places. But it is correct that having had time to review all of the documents that I cite in my own report, I have since finishing this report encountered a couple of other passages which suggest, in contradiction of this RS MUP document, that there may have been as many as, I forget the exact number, I'm sure you can give it to me, as many as 140 or -- it's a number in the low hundreds were allegedly still working in the ministry at that time. And those numbers would certainly tend to contradict the RS MUP document which mentions only six non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Like my colleague, I prepared a binder of documents, and I would like to ask the usher for assistance. Could we call P160 in the meantime. In your binder it's document number 3. In B/C/S it's page 5. In English it's 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's a speech by Mr. Zupljanin in the Serbian. It's the fourth paragraph from the top. In English third paragraph from the top. Mr. Zupljanin says there are about 8.500 active duty and reserve members in the region at the moment including 142 members of other ethnicities. I apologise to the interpreters for speaking too fast. This is that much-talked-about meeting on the 11th of July in Belgrade. Do you agree that it's mentioned in the report that Mr. Zupljanin indeed said this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, and that was the approximately 140 number that I thought you were going to mention, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So that we don't have to take Stojan Zupljanin at his word, let's look at 2D02-0503, and in your binder it's number 2. We received this document officially from the Banja Luka CSB this last autumn, and it is a list of employees and payroll dated October 1992. Only the first page and the last page have been translated, as is the custom with our translation service, and the names have not been translated. However, my assistant underlined all the names of non-Serbs who were employed in the MUP in October 1992. Therefore, I will ask to you look at the B/C/S version, and you will find a lot of Muslim and Croat names. And I assume if you see names like Anto or Muhamed or Selem, you recall be able to identify them as people of Croat or Muslim ethnicity. So please look at the underlined names. Those that are marked, could you confirm that they are Muslims or Croats.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm that many of the highlighted names in the B/C/S document are Croat or Muslim. I cannot say that all of them are because, as you know, you cannot always make that determination solely based on a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then on the basis of this document, would you be prepared to correct your report in the place where it says that only six non-Serbs were employed in the MUP at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly again grateful to you for this opportunity. As you know, the October 1992 pay lists are not ones that I've seen previously. But I agree with you that Mr. Zupljanin's statement with the, I think, 142 non-Serbs which, you know, theoretically could include Hungarians and Ukrainians as well as Muslims and Croats is valid. So I think that again that paragraph of the executive summary should be modified accordingly. I do want to underline, and this is very important, that the statement about six, only six non-Serbs being in RS MUP at the end of June 1992 is directly quoted from an RS MUP document. So that is obviously an open question why they were so off on their own count.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Most likely the minister was misinformed like you were as to the number of non-Serbs. That speaks a little about the accuracy of the reports that reach the minister from lower levels. But this was not a question, just my comment. Earlier today my colleague Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, could we get an exhibit number for this last document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 2D34, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]
