utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Zecevic, asked you about the event at Koricanska Stijena, and you discussed it with him a little, but I will go a little deeper. Since you worked at one time in the Office of the Prosecutor and you are familiar with procedures from your work, you are familiar with the police procedure of detecting and investigating and prosecuting. I mean, as a person who has had access to documents like this and to people who deal with this matter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one attains familiarity with such procedures from looking at these documents and the relevant laws and regulations, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then you might agree with me that the first thing to do when bodies are found and on-site investigation is carried out, the appropriate service identifies the bodies and then the site, the crime scene is secured?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that an on-site investigation is carried out by the prosecutor and the investigating judge in order to continue with the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is you who is the expert here, so yes, I agree and I am guided by your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then after these first steps have been taken, a criminal complaint is filed so that the prosecutor's office can get involved, and then under the leadership of the prosecutor and the investigating judge, perpetrators are identified as well as the circumstances under which the crime was committed, and then the whole criminal procedure continues from there.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The investigating judge and the prosecutor after receiving the criminal complaint issue instructions to the police as to what steps to take and how to gather information and evidence on the case, and they practically lead the case. Just a little correction: The investigating judge and the prosecutor, I said.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 1D00-2693.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, that's a criminal report that you don't have in the binder. I'll hand it to you now with the help of the usher. I believe you have seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I've seen this particular document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just scan it, please. It's a criminal complaint filed to the prosecutor's office by the Security Services Centre signed, Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if you look at this criminal complaint bearing mind the standard procedure prevailing in Republika Srpska at the time, you will agree that this whole procedure has been fully observed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does seem to conform to the procedure that you described, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And there is no doubt that these criminal charges referred to here are charges of a war crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again with the caveat that I'm not a lawyer, I see that the charge here is murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We are not talking about the qualification. The criminal charges are of murder, but the perpetrator hasn't been identified yet, and the bodies have not been identified yet. It's practically a criminal complaint for a war crime regardless of what it's called here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's argumentative. The document speaks for itself. It says murder under a particular provision of Criminal Code; it doesn't say war crime. This witness has said he is not a lawyer, not a legal expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try this another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that my client Stojan Zupljanin, among other things, is charged with this incident, Koricanska Stijena, and this Prosecution calls it a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, because we are operating under a different statute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my question was only whether this crime concerning which my client filed criminal charges is the same incident as described in the indictment against my client, that was the point of my question, just the yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the witness able to answer yes or no to that question? If so, he may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot answer that with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that this incident at Koricanska Stijena is included in the indictment against my client?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am ware that that incident is named in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that he is charged with failure to take appropriate steps or to file a criminal complaint, that that is the charge against my client?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He is not charged with failing to file a complaint. He is charged with failing to take adequate measures against the perpetrators. And again, these are legal submissions and things for Your Honours to decide, not something for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, having regard to the expertise of this witness, I'm not sure that I follow your -- where you are going, Mr. Krgovic, with this line of questions. This is addition to Mr. Hannis's point about the submissions and arguments which the document in question may form the basis of at an appropriate stage. How can -- as I said, I'm not sure how this witness can assist by addressing the point you are making on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this expert, police expert in his paragraph 353 says that the Security Services Centre failed to file reports or a criminal complaint against anyone but one suspect in war crimes and that there are no mention -- references to war crimes in the relevant period of the indictment. And that's why I believe it's relevant, because he deals with it in his report. And if you look at this report and admit it into evidence, the Trial Chamber will have his report before them including this statement that the CSB or the national security centre did not start a single case to prosecute war crimes. Therefore, I'm trying to establish what this expert understands to constitute a war crime, and I want to put specific examples before him. And the Court, and this is already a legal submission, is bound by the factual description of the Prosecutor, not that provided by a policeman. You have heard about this from witness Delic. And the Court in deliberating back in our system is not bound by anything but the factual description. That was the point of my question. Because at the beginning when I established that when the witness mentions war crimes, he speaks of war crimes not as an expert but as a regular person, and that is why I want to show some more documents to this witness regarding his finding in paragraph 353.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, then my objection is the question should be more directed specifically to what is in 353 and where it came from. This criminal complaint is for murder, and all it says is that unknown perpetrators were involved and there are a hundred bodies in the bottom of the canyon. At this point in time, that's not identified as a war crime. That could be 100 bodies in the bottom of the canyon as a result of some combat activity in the area possibly. But the CSB, the police, had the opportunity to identify certain crimes as war crimes and file them as such because apparently they did file one such crime, but this one was not one of those, as least not in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I suspect that the quickest way out of this is to allow Mr. Krgovic to proceed. Clearly there is room for disputation here. But I think I understand the basis on which Mr. Krgovic is asking this question. And if I appear to be tentative, it's because I am, because I heard what he has it to say, and I think I follow him. So please proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, on the first page of this document you will see a reference to a convoy of refugees who were going from Prijedor and Sanski Most towards Travnik. Do you agree with me? You nodded, but it was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on page 2 of this document it is said that the employees of the CSB will take all the operative measures to identify and apprehend the perpetrators; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I agree that that is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your report you mentioned several dispatches following this event, and this happened on the 8th of September, 1992. In your report, you mentioned a letter that my client Stojan Zupljanin sent to Prijedor to find out who was in the escort of this convoy. Do you remember mentioning this? The page -- that page is missing in my copy of the report. Do you remember that? You answered a question by Mr. Zecevic about this.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Stojan Zupljanin, as I state in my report, asked for information about the killings on several occasions in orders to Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as you said today to Mr. Zecevic, the response came that these persons were now involved in combat activities and they were not available?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It should be noted that it was at that point in time, that is to say, in the second half of August 1992, clear to both Mr. Drljaca and to Mr. Zupljanin that these unknown perpetrators were employees of the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that based on this criminal complaint and based on the evidence gathered at the time, the prosecution was started after the war against the perpetrators and they were tried in Banja Luka or Sarajevo, I'm not sure but you mentioned it earlier in your evidence.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned that I am aware of the fact that many years later, there were arrests and trials of those who were alleged to have participated in these killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And speaking of criminal complaints and the taking of measures, are you aware that the normal practice in the MUP of Republika Srpska, specifically in Banja Luka, in view of the specific circumstances of war, the practice was that professional members of the MUP would do their job and produce certain documents that could serve as a basis for Prosecution later on when the right conditions are created with no statute of limitations or fear thereof because the crimes concerned were grave?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that is the logical corollary to what Mr. Zecevic referred to and Mr. Cvijetic referred to as the dropping of the statute of limitations for crimes committed by police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I'm not going to deal with this criminal report any longer, can we please have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D35, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please call up Exhibit 280 65 ter. And it's number 7 in your binder, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 1. That's an analysis of the work of the public security station of Banja Luka in 1992, that's Banja Luka CSB. Can you please look at the signature on the last page. This is a report submitted by inspectors, and you reviewed this document when drafting your report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please have page 5 in B/C/S and page 6 in English. In B/C/S it's the first paragraph from the top, and in English it's the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I spoke about, and you agree with me that the practice was such that we have a description here of the procedure applicable in investigating crimes. Would you agree with me that this is what it says in this report, that this was a widespread practice in the area covered by the Security Services Centre of Banja Luka; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this document paints a portrait of what crimes were taking place in the operational area of SJB Banja Luka during this period and that it also discusses what was done to combat such crime. Excuse me, CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D36, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is this a convenient time for the break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is near that time, but in as much as we started a little late, if you have one or two questions to run it for another five minutes, we can take the break then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you will agree with me, and by reading your report, I noticed a number of problems that affected the work of MUP of Republika Srpska in 1992, including the Banja Luka CSB. And I'm going to enumerate these problems and ask you whether you would agree with that or not, but generally speaking there were quite a few problems that disrupted the work of the MUP during the war. First of all, let's begin with the first specific problem which was the lack of professional personnel as a result of the separation of MUP into the Muslim and Serb portions, and that a number of Muslim members of the MUP ceased to work there by either joining the Muslim MUP or simply by resigning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly was one of the problems faced. I don't think I would in it's entirety agree with your characterisation of why the Muslim members of the MUP ceased to work there. But certainly the fact that the CSB was, with the exceptions you have mentioned, largely without Muslim and Croat employees meant a deficit that was, to some extent, remedied by an influx of Serbs, police officers from Croatia where they had been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Among those peoples who were admitted into MUP, this was done indiscriminately without any vetting procedure?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I note in my report, for the ministry as a whole and certainly also in the area of CSB Banja Luka and with specific reference to a statement made by Mr. Stanisic, the unfortunate fact was that the ministry as a whole was quite indiscriminate in admitting people into employment in 1992 without appropriate vetting procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The next problem that considerably made the functioning of the MUP difficult refers to this Rump Banja Luka CSB which means that police units were often taken by the army, resubordinated to the army, and used for combat operations instead of for carrying out regular police work; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All reports of the RS MUP throughout 1992 including on the territory of CSB Banja Luka reflect the enormous strain placed on the police by it's extensive involvement in combat activity which left logically comparatively little time and resources for traditional police work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the participation of the organs, the courts and other organs, particularly with reference to public law and order, the misdemeanour courts were virtually non-functioning, therefore, the commission of misdemeanours most often committed by conscript could not have been properly sanctioned by misdemeanour courts. I'm referring to this same document, page 3 in B/C/S, where it speaks about public law and order. It specifically speaks about law and order, and I'm going to read it out to you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please indicate which paragraph he is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters are asking you to identify which paragraph you are reading out from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is page 3 in B/C/S, second paragraph entitled "Public Law and Order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "Often under the influence of alcohol and with the usage of fire-arms, they disturb public law and order and thereby jeopardise the safety of citizens, and frequently they oppose as a group or individually anyone who tries to stop them. Since these are conscripts, members of the OUP are very often reluctant to undertake any measures or are very slow or inefficient, and which is even worse, they express solidarity with the perpetrators which has devastating effects on the public law and order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Have you formulated -- sorry. I wasn't sure whether you had formulated the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this picture portrayed in this report and you, yourself, partly mentioned it in your report is a true portrayal of the situation prevalent on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this is an accurate portrayal of the situation on the ground. It's a portrayal which goes again and again in numerous RS MUP reports. And just to wrap up on a previous point, when you talk about the military involvement on the territory of the police, on the territory of CSB Banja Luka, it is worth noting that the RS MUP draft 1992 annual report states that the CSB Banja Luka had by far the most extensive combat involvement of any CSB in the RS in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I begin with the witness, I was rather hastily putting my question, 56, line 13, I said that security organs were very slow and inefficient. I was reading this very quickly, and that changed the whole meaning of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But I guess Mr. Nielsen, you understood what I wanted to say in light of this recent correction that I've made?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, and we see that in the document that we were looking at that in the opinion of the -- of CSB Banja Luka, the military organs were ineffective.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if you look at the next paragraph that deals with crime rates, this more or less repeats your answer given to Mr. Cvijetic, that is to say, it describes who are mainly the perpetrators of these crimes, that these are actually members of the military, and there is a description of how they are being processed.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this report, certainly military conscripts are a major source of crime. Other groups that are frequently mentioned are of course members of paramilitary groups and just the general rise in criminality because of a very bad security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you would agree with me if I say that these issues mentioned in this report were mentioned for the first time at the meeting of the 11th of July held in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may have been the first time that those issues were mentioned at that high a level of the ministry. However, documents from April, May, and June, and the first half of July show that the officials in the police were permanently concerned about the deteriorating security situation, in particular about the enormous explosion in criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In his speech delivered on the 11th of July, Stojan Zupljanin was the first person to raise these issues. To that end, could you please look at P160. Page 5 in B/C/S and page -- actually, pages 7 to 8. It starts on page 7 and then goes on, on page 8 in English. Would you agree with me that Mr. Zupljanin speaks here about the work of the army and Crisis Staffs and says that they are collecting Muslim population and placing them in the camps and then the MUP is requested to provide security, and this is the first time that someone without any pressure from the international community highlighted the problem of the conditions in these detention centres, and proposed -- and initiated this problem to be resolved; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an analyst, it's my job to be very specific, so yes, I agree with you that Mr. Zupljanin speaks about the issues that you mentioned, and that is reflected in the document we have in front of us. As to whether that is indeed the first time that someone, as you say, without any pressure from the international community highlighted this problem, that is a finding that I'm unable to concur with because I don't have the information that would lead me to such a conclusion. He certainly does highlight the issue though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in preparing your report, you haven't found any proof that he [as interpreted] was done under the pressure of the international community and that that problem had already been in the public domain? I am talking about the Banja Luka Krajina, specifically.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any information to suggest -- that suggests that Mr. Zupljanin was making his comments under duress or pressure of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In one of the following paragraphs, it's the fourth one from the bottom, he speaks about the army and says that the army is -- are asking for resubordination of the entire force. And then he tackles other subjects as well, and you said that these issues stretch throughout the whole period, but the gist of my question was that all these issues were for the for the first time raised by Mr. Zupljanin, and in order to avoid the influence of the local authorities who are actually paying the police, try to interfere into the chain of command over the MUP. You would agree with me that this is the essence of the objections concerning the system of financing the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the financing of the MUP by Crisis Staffs and other local authorities was a major issue during this period. I don't know if it was Mr. Zupljanin or another participant at this meeting, but someone at had meeting certainly said that he who pays the piper chooses the tune, and that was one reason why MUP needed to be financed at the ministerial and state budget level and not at the local level. I would point out that Mr. Zupljanin's statements are somewhat at odds with his instructions in June 1992 to his own subordinates that they should very faithfully follow the instructions of the local and regional Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 it says that the function -- the system of functioning has been broken up.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I noted previously, communications issues were -- and difficulties with communications were certainly discussed at this meeting, including by Mr. Zupljanin, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning your previous answer when you mentioned a letter and the execution of police tasks, have you found any document? And I'm talking about later period July, he sent a letter to the police stations, instructed them not to carry out the orders of local authorities that refer to the security of detention centres and other tasks of that nature.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've stated several is times, it is generally the case that after June 1992 there is a major policy change in MUP regarding whether or not to take orders from Crisis Staffs. And as we see at this meeting and in the conclusions that follow out from this meeting, and Mr. Zupljanin emulates this in his own orders, the trend after June 1992 is to centralise decision-making within the organs of Internal Affairs and to tell the Crisis Staffs that they are no longer to give orders or otherwise interfere with the work of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was primarily for the reason of many police stations being under the influence of their local Crisis Staff and their environment that they didn't follow MUP instructions, but rather followed the instructions of the Crisis Staff who were on many occasions in contravention with the instructions received from the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is definitely the case that the minister as well as Mr. Zupljanin wished to prevent situations which had been occurring in which the Crisis Staffs had been ordering the police do things that they should not be doing according to, for example, the Law on Internal Affairs. So that this is, again, after June 1992, part of a concerted effort to rectify that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later on you could see and you mentioned it in your analysis concerning the proposals put forth by Mr. Zupljanin, certain concrete measures and steps were taken in order to implement them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. As I've noted previously, this meeting of the 11th of July resulted in a very specific document issued, I believe, on the 17th of July in which various organisations within MUP were specifically tasked to implement the conclusions of this meeting, and of course, Mr. Zupljanin participated in such implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One of the problems that I noticed that you mentioned, but not so emphatically, was that certain public security stations did not obey the orders, or let's say guide-lines and instructions received either from the centre of the securities because the structure and the organisation of the MUP was somewhat different from the one of the army. Although, you are not an expert in this particular field, one often uses terms control, co-operation, harmonisation, et cetera, which in war time can only make the functioning of the MUP difficult, the usage of such terms and such approach in operation.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that one of the problems that contributes to this situation at the level of the municipal public security stations is that for the period until the 11 July meeting, they are being told certainly in the northwestern Bosnia, the Bosnian Krajina, by Mr. Zupljanin as the top police official that they are to heed and implement instructions, orders, that are issued to them by the Crisis Staffs at the municipal and regional level. Whereas after the 11th of July, they are told that they should only receive orders and implement instructions that are coming through the police organs. So this was a situation that was changing, and it was certainly a situation that was in contradiction of the way in which they had been operating from the beginning of April until the end of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because the situation was out of control, and that was one of the conclusions of the 11th of July meeting, that is to place all police forces under centralised control and to bring some order into the functioning of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one says that something is out of control, that seems to me to suggest that no one was in control. What I'm saying is, rather, that for the period from early April until the end of June, it was in many cases the Crisis Staffs that were in control. And I remind the Court again that police officers were members of these Crisis Staffs. The problem that accumulated was that the Crisis Staffs in many cases were asking the police to do certain tasks without first consulting with the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and in some cases, as I said, they were tasking them to do things that were outside the jurisdiction of the police. In line with what I call re-centralisation or centralisation of Internal Affairs in the RS, after June 1992 this situation had to be remedied and everyone in the ministry seemed to agree about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: However, the situation did not improve significantly. Therefore, I would like you to look at document 266 from 65 ter list. It's a minute of the meeting of an extended collegium of the minister of the interior. It's your number 5. You have mentioned this document in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please move, or, rather, turn to page 4 in the Serbian version and page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the fifth paragraph from the top below this encircled one. It says that from -- within the remit of the work organisation and internal organisation of units and the job description of employees, such formulations such as co-ordination and dovetailing, et cetera, should be removed and emphasis should be laid on direct command and control role of superior officer as well as the responsibility of each employee for the tasks that he or she is supposed to carry out. This is basically what I asked you about a minute ago. That is to say, to chuck out all these terms that lower units used as an excuse to avoid the implementation of the instructions received from the superior organs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that this reflects this ongoing struggle to stream-line and make more consistent the way in which the ministry functioned. As with, for example, the ministry's protracted struggle with paramilitary organisations, so it was with the Crisis Staffs. This was a procedure which was often going two steps back, one step forward, but was moving in the direction that you highlight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, you would agree that it was very difficult, or rather difficult for the MUP to operate and carry out its general duties as provided by the law?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that the way in which you just characterised the situation conforms with the way the RS MUP characterises the overall situation in which it operated in 1992 in all its analytical summary reports including the draft 1992 annual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, in your report you described the functioning of the national security service, and it relates to a number of reports that you refer to. You said that from April 1992 until the end of that year, the security sector at the CSB accused only one individual for war crimes. And that in the relevant annual report for 1992, there is not a single mention of any war crimes committed against non-Serbian population. You would agree with me that regardless of these two documents, there is evidence that the state security service was very much involved in detecting crimes against the Muslims; is that right? If you look at other documents that are not strictly related to this specific paragraph.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to make it very clear that the statement in paragraph 353, which you allude to, is purely a statement about what the SNB, the national security service was doing with respect to war crimes, and not a statement about what CSB Banja Luka, as a whole, of which the SNB was only one part, was doing. This is just a finding that comes straight out of the document that I cite in footnote 532. I agree with you that the SNB in the course of 1992 did look into war crimes on a regular basis, including on several occasions war crimes, alleged war crimes committed against the Muslims and Croats. And I note that I have cited a number of reports, mostly from early 1993, in which the national security service in the Banja Luka and Prijedor areas among other things catalogue the destruction of mosques and Catholic churches in northwestern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly look at 2D27. It's number 1 in your binder. I don't know, Mr. Nielsen, if you had occasion to see this document before. The B/C/S copy is a bit illegible. There is a translation in the attachment. But first of all tell me, did you see this before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have seen this before, I note that it's from Teslic municipality. This may have been, although my memory is vague on this point, among the documents related to the group popularly referred to as the Mice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. And this is a criminal complaint against several persons, I believe there are sixteen of them, plus their leader, who is on the run, and they are reported for widespread looting and plunder against Muslims and Croats, that's on page 3 in B/C/S; illegal arrests, that's on page 4 in B/C/S; and page 5, keeping large numbers of Muslims and Croats in inhumane conditions, beatings, illegal arrests, and finally the killing of a number of persons of Muslim and Croat ethnicity by this group on the premises of the public security station and some other locations. This is my summary, but I see that you are following because you read very fast. It's all in the attachments, I don't have them, but all these statements are indicated there. It's a very voluminous and detailed criminal report, if you will agree with me.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the B/C/S version, please and the signature. We can't see it in the English, but the name is Predrag Radulovic. It's only in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the last page of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, the last but one. It's enlarged on the screen in front of you. Predrag Radulovic was a member of the state security service; correct? And you will find him in those reports about the Milos group. He signed those dispatches. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall long discussions about Mr. Radulovic and his association with the group that called itself Milos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he was a member of the state security service, later national security service?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until about 1994 when he then, I believe, offered his services to the Serbian state security services in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This concerns an event from July 1992 when he was a member of the state security service; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you then modify your findings in paragraph 353 where you said that the state security service, later national security service, never filed a single criminal complaint concerning a war crime? Would you -- perhaps not modified, but supplemented, I'm sorry if I misspoke. You don't need to modify it, but perhaps supplement your report to say that at least one criminal report against a number of persons was filed concerning a war crime?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I note that in at least the English version of paragraph 353 which I wrote, I stated that "from April 1992 until the end of that year, the SNB sector at CSB Banja Luka pressed charges against only one individual for suspected war crimes." Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There are at least 16 of them?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is certainly correct. Where I would perhaps take issue with your characterization or the need to rewrite or amend my finding is whether these people in this document are actually charged with war crimes, just as we discussed earlier, the one for Koricanska Stijena where it says murder, I don't see the word war crime. Again, let me be very clear that the finding, if that's what you want to call it, that the SNB sector at CSB Banja Luka pressed charges against one individual is their finding not mine. I'm just quoting it from their document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely for that reason I asked my first question, if you remember, what exactly you understand war crime to mean. I did not mean to offend you, I just wanted to find out to what extent we agree on the terms, although the Prosecutor objected and I could not continue. That was the point anyway. Basically this is a war crime, that's the whole story.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, in testifying here, and again hyper-conscious of the fact that I'm not a lawyer as yourself, I'm not making any findings at any point in time and do not wish to make any findings about whether any act constitutes a war crime or not. I may have my own opinions about that. I'll keep those to myself. But at any rate, I'm trying to adequately and accurately tell the Court what these documents say. So when they say war crime or when they say illegal, then I quote that. I make no finding about whether that was actually case. I do find again, as we note, we are dealing with professional police officers unlike myself, and I assume that they have some idea about what was legal and illegal and what constituted a war crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and since you are not qualified properly for police terms, you quote them in the documents as you find them without interpreting them and going deeper into their meaning.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because ultimately this is a report about what the police did and how they perceived their own work, and I'm very glad that you raised that point because in December I was asked about so-called loyalty oaths. Your colleagues told me and instructed me hopefully that that was not an official term being used. But if you see the police documents themselves, the police themselves use that term, statements of loyalty, even though it apparently has no legal significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you will agree with me that this event and these incidents in Krstici are part of the indictment against my client?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read the indictment for quite some time, but if you say that is in the indictment, I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Basically we agreed on this passage that -- I understood you were saying that -- are saying that when SNB did not prosecute a war crime, when you say that, you don't mean that the SNB did nothing to collect evidence or did not take any steps et cetera, and in that sense you would modify this particular passage in your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that assumes a fact I think is not in evidence yet. He is referring to paragraph 353 of Mr. Nielsen's report where cites from April 1992 until the end of the year, the SNB sector at CSB Banja Luka pressed charges against only one individual. He hasn't established that this document that appears to have the signature of Predrag Radulovic was from the SNB sector at CSB Banja Luka. You may recall some evidence that we've had already, and I'm sure you'll hear more, that there was a dispute about whether Teslic pertained to Doboj CSB or Banja Luka CSB. The English translation I've seen of the document says the signature, Predrag Radulovic's signature is "on behalf of," and then it says, "illegible." So we don't know if it's on behalf of CSB Banja Luka or CSB Doboj or some other organisation. So we haven't established that fact yet to warrant asking this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my learned friend is wrong, we did ask to the witness, the protected witness which I cross-examined him and it's related, he confirmed that Predrag Radulovic was member of SNB Banja Luka, if you remember. And he spoke with Mr. Radulovic during the inspection of the -- and if we can go to the private session, I can tell the name of this witness, just to remind the Prosecution if it's necessary. But if Mr. Nielsen agree with me that -- oh, he is under the oath, I mean, Mr. Nielsen. So, he signed the undertaking, so I think I can do that in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you continue in your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour, because no matter what that answer is it doesn't change the fact that the source of Mr. Nielsen's statement is a report from CSB Banja Luka. And until he establishes that somebody in CSB Banja Luka has considered Mr. Radulovic as being a member of the SNB in Banja Luka at the time that this report was submitted and he was working on behalf of CSB Banja Luka, then that doesn't make Mr. Nielsen's statement inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is that dispute, that Mr. Radulovic didn't work in SNB Banja Luka on that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know where all Mr. Radulovic worked, and on -- in what position he was doing this. I seem to recall seeing some document where he was acting as SJB chief for Teslic for a brief period of time. So I don't know on whose behalf and in what capacity he is writing this document at this time. I don't think that's been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you look in the appendix of your indictment you can find the position of Mr. Radulovic very clear within the organisation of the SNB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's in the prosecutor's chart that he is SNB Banja Luka Milos group. Isn't that enough, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you'll need to hear some further testimony about what Mr. Radulovic was during at certain periods of time to determine whether or not when this criminal report was filed whether it was filed on behalf of SNB Banja Luka or on behalf of some other organisation, such as headquarters or SNB in Doboj, because Mr. Nielsen's report is referring to a report from CSB Banja Luka. And whoever wrote the report in CSB Banja Luka either didn't consider Mr. Radulovic as part of the SNB or else they didn't have this report in front of them when they wrote their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, just answer my first question, if he is aware where Mr. Radulovic is working, if he confirmed he was in SNB until 1994. I mean, so he has knowledge about it. So I can't see any sense of this objection. If you look at two pages before, I clearly asked Mr. Nielsen what was the position of Mr. Radulovic on this period, relevant period of time, I mean, July 1992. And he clearly said, yes, he was working in SNB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Without further confusing the issue and getting lost in all these details, the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we are wasting time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No, no, I was going to say, Mr. Krgovic, as the question is originally phrased by you before Mr. Hannis intervened, would the witness -- as I understand your question is whether the witness would modify his answer in the light of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a question that he may or may not be able it to answer so let's deal with that and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just to indicate, Your Honour, it was my understanding that Mr. Radulovic was temporarily appointed as chief of the SJB Teslic I think at the time this criminal report was charged. And therefore he is issuing the report on behalf of the SJB and not the SNB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Unless I've lost the point of Mr. Krgovic's question, Mr. Hannis, it seems to me that the identity of the individual is less important than the -- than what the document purports to say and whether the witness would modify his answer in light of the contents of the document. Isn't that the question, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking at the document which you've provided to me, it is the case that it's a criminal complaint for things that, as you state, some may construe as war crimes. It is issued by, if you look at the letterhead, the public security station in Teslic and signed by Mr. Radulovic. It does not mention in the document, as far as I can see, the national security service, even though I do not contest that Mr. Radulovic was at that time also an employee of the SNB. But ultimately, it does not really modify my one sentence in paragraph 353 because all I'm saying is a simple case of an analyst saying, This is what that document says, period. Now, the authors of that document might be wrong, but that should be put to the authors of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which brings me to another thing. When you made that conclusion, you did not look at other documents than the two you mentioned; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the context of discussions of the RS MUP's interest in prosecuting individuals for war crimes, I, as an analyst, thought that it was salient to quote the Banja Luka SNB sector's report on its own work for 1992 which includes that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, among other things, your report deals with Manjaca. You will agree with me that Manjaca was a military camp under the exclusive jurisdiction of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that Manjaca was a military detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it was exclusively the corps commander and the army that had responsibility for this detention facility; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding, and it is my understanding based on police documentation that the corps commander on occasion allowed police personnel to interrogate individuals detained in Manjaca together with the military investigative and police authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in the functioning of Manjaca camp, that was the only police role if we set aside the dozen or so policemen who provided security?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that besides very limited guarding of Manjaca providing security, as you put it, and the interrogation of prisoners at Manjaca by the SNB together with their military colleagues, the police's role at Manjaca was very limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the police had no influence whatsoever of the organisation of the camp, the way it operated, the conditions inside. It was solely within the purview of military authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the -- as you state, the conditions and the way in which Manjaca operated was under the control of military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, the army made efforts to exert influence and to control other detention facilities; right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that. From the police's perspective, as we discussed earlier today, the problem was rather that sometimes the army did not show any interest in some of the other detention facilities and left the police to operate them instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the witness 1D12. That's 65 ter 503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the previous one and the one before that, the one before that being 65 ter 266, you don't tender them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, it's not in your binder. [In English] Usher, can you provide this to the witness. I apologise, I didn't get this because I was concentrating on the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, while we are sorting out this document, I note that we have 20 minutes left before we rise for the day. You would recall that this witness is only available until tomorrow, and tomorrow is reserved for re-examination by the Prosecution. And I am reminded that you had indicated that Mr. Pantelic also had questions in cross-examination, and I am appreciative of the fact that about 30 minutes of today's session at the very beginning was taken up with certain procedural matters, but the -- well, I don't really have a question, but I'm just alerting you to where we are in terms of time, in terms of what the completion of the cross-examination of this witness on behalf of Zupljanin and the fact that tomorrow is reserved for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is my last question, so if I am going to count, I still have one hour to complete this cross-examination, meaning Zupljanin team in total has one hour, if I'm correct, so this is my last question. So Mr. Pantelic will continue, so we'll see how far we come to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nielsen, have you had occasion to see this document before?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I've seen this document because it's cited by Mr. Brown in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This document shows that Mr. Talic is ordering Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor that an inspection is pending. He gives them orders what to do in preparation and issues an order basically; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this is precisely on the issue of army interest and involvement. It is the army here who is seeking to control and to instruct these detention facilities that are not within the system of military detention facilities, but the army is still trying to exert influence?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether it's an order or not, what he is doing is he is informing CSB Prijedor which is obviously -- which actually is not a CSB at that point but is rather an SJB. But he is informing the police in Prijedor that he has approved the visit of the international commission, what is the -- the international commission for visiting prisoners detained at detention camps at Manjaca, Trnopolje, Omarska, and Prijedor, and he is informing them that they better get their house in order by the time this commission shows up. That, to me, does not mean that he is asserting exclusive control of those authorities, and the very fact that he sends to the police in Prijedor, shows his knowledge of the fact that the police are involved in running some of those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: He is doing that, in fact, pursuant to a verbal order by the commander of the Main Staff who approved this visit. It seems from the document that it was General Mladic who approved this visit to detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in addition to the CSB Prijedor, this document is sent to the security organ which, if you are aware of the whole structure, is involved in guarding duties and security in detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The organs of security of the 1st Krajina Corps are among the recipients of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have an exhibit number for this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Nielsen, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document has already been assigned Exhibit 1D12, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Thank you for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Danish is impeccable, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Like your Serbian language. Mr. Nielsen, you stated on many occasions during the examination-in-chief and cross-examination and in earlier proceedings that you are not an expert in legal matters; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and as we say in Danish, I'm now stating that for the 117th time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you are not an expert in military issues?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ditto.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you are not an expert in political issues?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that certainly depends on what you mean by political issues. I have written extensively on political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You are not a political analyst?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a degree in political science and in international relations, and so political analysis is certainly part of my purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So I can take that you are an expert for political life in Bosnia and Herzegovina; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the purposes of that case that's not the way I understand that I'm being proffered as a witness particularly because, as I stated previously, the political landscape and situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina was dealt with in a complimentary report by Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I take it that you are not an expert for political life in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he has not been tendered by the Prosecution in this case as a political expert, he is being tendered as a police expert. Many of these questions have already been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Nielsen, you stated that you are not an expert in international public law, I believe?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you are historian, you have a PhD degree in philosophy; am I right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are wrong, I have a PhD in history, which is called a doctor of philosophy, as are all PhDs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So would you agree me, Mr. Nielsen, that having in mind that all these issues that you just mentioned, that it would be fair to actually extract from your report everything which is related to police matters, to political issues, to military issues, or constitutional law issues; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Argumentative, Your Honour. That's matter for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, in preparing your report, you were actually working on the basis to support Prosecution case; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated at the outset of my testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, just give me yes or no answer, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that case, no, you are incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, can we agree upon the fact that MUP being a part of government, now we are speaking about Republika Srpska, actually is organised in accordance and it's functioning is in accordance with the law on state administration? Am I correct or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I responded to that previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me if I will put to you that the notion of functioning of MUP is actually closer to the verb to direct and not to command like in army structure? In fact, Mr. Nielsen, this is the approach which was taken by many of Trial Chambers within this Tribunal. Would you agree with me or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand your question, quite frankly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will try to be more precise. We have two meanings of functioning. We have verb "to direct," and we have verb "to command." It's understandable for you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Verb "to command" is more related to the army than to police; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In normal peacetime circumstances, that would be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So in police work, we could say that the function of the police is related to the notion of direction rather than commanding; yes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I don't think that a police officer who disobeys the commands or instructions of his superior officer will last very long in professional service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We shall come to that. At this point it is quite enough. During your testimony in examination-in-chief, this is transcript page 4749 until page -51, in your answers on Honourable Judge Harhoff questions regarding the role of the police during military operations, you were explaining that actually, I'm quoting, you said beaurocratically speaking, during some combat activities police being subordinated to respective military commander is the fact, but on the other hand this member of police is also in kind of command relation with the MUP. Do you remember that issue that was mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, I put to you, Dr. Nielsen, that during military operations only military commander in its zone of responsibility of his unit is responsible for command and not police officers or employees of Ministry of Internal Affairs. Do you agree with me or not? Just yes or no question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and neither does the defence expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Give me the answer on the following situation: If during military operation a member of police unit commit a crime, who is in charge to initiate proceedings against him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding is that responsibility rests with the military authorities for that case that you explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And another issue that I would like to discuss with you is, would you agree with me that the work of CSB Banja Luka with regard to the communication and sending dispatches and daily reports and weekly reports so that CSB Banja Luka was more active than the other regions primarily due to the problems that the other regions have with the communications; am I correct or not?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to actually answer that question for the reason that I note in my report that we in this institution, the ICTY, have a surplus of information, documentation from CSB Banja Luka, whereas we have comparatively little from other CSBs. So it's difficult to make that finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In any case, CSB Banja Luka, I would say, in quite good order informed and received -- informed MUP and received direction from MUP; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is what I stated earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And you stated in paragraph 236 of your report that -- actually you are describing the way how this reporting process is going, and then you mentioned in paragraph 237 that Mr. Zupljanin actually in order to comply with this practice, in fact, Mr. Zupljanin reprimanded chiefs of SJB for submitting poor daily reports, that was the fact actually from the documents that you were reviewing. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is an issue between quantity and quality here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. It is not for us to discuss that matter. Now, in the paragraph 186 of your report, you are speaking about the CSB structure, but I'm taking -- I stand corrected, of course, that you -- in this particular paragraph you would use rule book of -- 1992 rule book of MUP; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this rule book was a draft made, I think, in, let's say -- where it was made this rule book?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we discussed yesterday, the draft, I believe, was finalised in September 1992, and it was adopted, I think, in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this particular rule book was related to the state of imminent threat of war and war, state of war; yes?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding, that it was drafted to conform with the operation of MUP in those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me that in other, I would say, circumstances actually MUP was information so they used former rule books, I believe, from Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina MUP; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agreed, and I answered that question earlier, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. And actually in accordance with this previous regulation, the structure of CSB was in general terms the following: On the top was the chief of CSB; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then he got actually a certain department and a certain services, two were most important under him was a chief of sector of national security or state security; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And on the other hand, his, I would say, assistant or colleague was chief of sector of public security; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And also chief of CSB was in charge for the various departments, I'm speaking about the CSB Banja Luka, department for finance; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And then other was department for legal affairs; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are again correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the other one was department for analytical affairs; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, it was the department for connection, transmission, and communications in general; yes? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, we've reached the point where we must rise for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you, and tomorrow I have additional time to finish with Mr. Nielsen, I believe. Because in the meantime, I was speaking with my learned friend, Mr. Hannis, in and general, he was keen to allocate certain couple of minutes, if necessary for me, or maybe I'm wrong. You never know with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Keen" might be too strong a word for it, but I'm not objecting to him having some additional time because we spent that half-hour at the beginning, I re-opened to do some additional redirect, so I think it's fair to subtract some time from me tomorrow, but I don't know how much time he is asking for, an hour, 45 minutes, or something in that neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: I would be comfortable maximum, I do my best, but maximum it will be around 45 minutes, something like that. So I will be along these lines, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, if we extract from that 45 minutes, the 10 minutes that you spent on irrelevant questions like you did in the beginning of this, then it will work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will do my best, Your Honour, to do my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
